article.title: Why Retry Logic Needs Exponential Backoff and Jitter
article.why: 理解錯誤的 retry 策略如何放大系統故障。
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

sources.label: AWS Architecture Blog — Exponential Backoff and Jitter

paragraphs.en:
Retries make distributed systems more reliable when failures are temporary. A network request may time out, a service may briefly exceed capacity, or a database connection may fail for a moment. Trying again can turn a transient failure into a successful operation. But poorly designed retries can make an outage worse.

Imagine that 10,000 clients call the same service. The service becomes overloaded and returns errors to all of them. If every client retries immediately, the service receives another huge wave of traffic before it has recovered. If they all wait exactly one second, they may still return together one second later. The clients become synchronized, creating repeated traffic spikes.

Exponential backoff reduces this pressure by increasing the delay after each failure. A client might wait one second after the first failure, two seconds after the second, four after the third, and so on, usually with a maximum cap. This gives the downstream system more time to recover and reduces the rate of repeated requests.

However, backoff alone can still leave many clients synchronized because they started failing at the same moment and calculate the same delays. Jitter adds randomness to the waiting time. Instead of every client retrying at exactly four seconds, they retry at different times within a defined range. The load becomes more spread out.

Retries should also be selective. Some errors are worth retrying, such as certain timeouts, connection resets, or server responses indicating temporary overload. Other errors are permanent until the request changes. Repeatedly retrying an invalid request or an authorization failure wastes capacity and delays useful error handling.

Idempotency matters when a request may have succeeded even though the client did not receive the response. Suppose a payment request reaches the server, the payment succeeds, but the response is lost. A blind retry could charge the customer twice. Idempotency keys or operation-specific safeguards allow repeated attempts to produce one intended effect.

A retry policy therefore needs several parameters: which errors are retryable, the initial delay, backoff multiplier, maximum delay, maximum attempts or total retry budget, jitter strategy, and request timeout. These settings should reflect the latency requirements and capacity of the systems involved.

Observability is equally important. Metrics should distinguish original requests from retry attempts. A service may appear to receive twice its normal traffic during an incident even though user demand did not change. Without retry metrics, teams can misdiagnose the source of the load.

Retries also operate across layers. An application library may retry three times, a service mesh may retry again, and a caller may repeat the whole operation. Multiplicative retries can create far more attempts than anyone intended. Teams should understand which layer owns retry behavior and avoid uncontrolled stacking.

The broader principle is that recovery behavior is part of system load. A failure does not reduce demand automatically; it can cause clients to generate more demand. Exponential backoff slows that feedback loop, while jitter prevents clients from moving in lockstep.

Good retry logic is therefore not simply “try again when something fails.” It is a controlled strategy for giving temporary failures another chance without overwhelming the system that is trying to recover. The best policy balances resilience, latency, safety, and capacity rather than maximizing the number of attempts.
paragraphs.zh: Retry 能處理暫時性故障，但立即或同步重試會形成 retry storm。Exponential backoff 拉長間隔，jitter 打散客戶端時間；同時還需限制可重試錯誤、總嘗試量並確保操作 idempotent。
paragraphs.ja: 再試行は一時障害に有効ですが、同時再試行は負荷を増幅します。指数バックオフで間隔を広げ、jitterで再試行時刻を分散し、冪等性や再試行対象も設計する必要があります。

quiz.question: Why is jitter useful in addition to exponential backoff?
quiz.answer: It prevents many clients from retrying at the same scheduled times.
